questions.lo: Gravity as a force between masses
questions.q: What is gravity?
options: A pushing force between all objects
A pulling (attractive) force between objects that have mass
A force that only acts on metal objects
A force that only exists on Earth
questions.explain: Gravity is a force of attraction that acts between all objects that have mass. The bigger the masses, and the closer they are, the stronger the pull.

questions.lo: The difference between mass and weight
questions.q: Which statement about mass and weight is correct?
options: Mass is a force measured in newtons
Weight is the amount of matter in an object
Mass is measured in kilograms; weight is a force measured in newtons
Mass and weight are two names for exactly the same thing
questions.explain: Mass (in kg) is the amount of matter in an object and never changes. Weight (in N) is the force of gravity pulling on that mass, so it changes with location.

questions.lo: The difference between mass and weight
questions.q: An astronaut with a mass of 70 kg travels from Earth to the Moon. What happens to their mass and weight on the Moon?
options: Both mass and weight stay the same
Mass stays the same, but weight decreases
Mass decreases, but weight stays the same
Both mass and weight decrease
questions.explain: Mass is the same everywhere, so it stays at 70 kg. The Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's, so the astronaut's weight (the force of gravity) decreases.

questions.lo: Using weight = mass x gravitational field strength (g)
questions.q: Which equation correctly links weight, mass and gravitational field strength?
options: weight = mass ÷ g
weight = mass × g
weight = mass + g
mass = weight × g
questions.explain: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = m × g). Weight is in newtons, mass in kilograms and g in N/kg.

questions.lo: Using weight = mass x gravitational field strength (g)
questions.q: A box has a mass of 15 kg. On Earth g = 10 N/kg. What is the box's weight on Earth?
questions.explain: W = m × g = 15 × 10 = 150 N. Multiply the mass in kg by g in N/kg to get the weight in newtons.

questions.lo: Using weight = mass x gravitational field strength (g)
questions.q: A student has a mass of 50 kg. Using g = 10 N/kg on Earth, what is the student's weight?
options: 5 N
questions.explain: W = m × g = 50 × 10 = 500 N. A common mistake is to give 50 N (that is the mass, not the weight).

questions.lo: Using weight = mass x gravitational field strength (g)
questions.q: An object weighs 240 N on Earth, where g = 10 N/kg. What is the object's mass?
options: 24 kg
240 kg
250 kg
questions.explain: Rearrange W = m × g to m = W ÷ g = 240 ÷ 10 = 24 kg.

questions.lo: Gravitational field strength on Earth and other worlds
questions.q: Roughly what is the gravitational field strength, g, on the surface of the Earth?
options: 1 N/kg
10 N/kg
100 N/kg
questions.explain: On Earth g is about 10 N/kg, meaning each kilogram of mass is pulled down with a force of about 10 N.

questions.lo: Gravitational field strength on Earth and other worlds
questions.q: A 20 kg toolkit is taken to the Moon, where g = 1.6 N/kg. What is its weight on the Moon?
questions.explain: W = m × g = 20 × 1.6 = 32 N. On Earth the same toolkit would weigh 200 N, because Earth's g is much larger.

questions.lo: Gravitational field strength on Earth and other worlds
questions.q: Why does the same object weigh more on Jupiter than on Earth?
options: The object gains mass on Jupiter
Jupiter is more massive, so its gravitational field strength is larger
Jupiter is closer to the Sun
There is no air resistance on Jupiter
questions.explain: Jupiter is far more massive than Earth, so its gravitational field strength (g) is bigger. The object's mass is unchanged, but W = m × g gives a larger weight.

questions.lo: The Sun as a star, galaxies and the Universe
questions.q: What type of object is the Sun?
options: A planet
A moon
A star
A galaxy
questions.explain: The Sun is a star — a huge ball of hot gas that gives out its own light. It only looks bigger and brighter than other stars because it is much closer to us.

questions.lo: The Sun as a star, galaxies and the Universe
questions.q: Which list is in order from smallest to largest?
options: Galaxy, star, Universe
Star, galaxy, Universe
Universe, galaxy, star
Star, Universe, galaxy
questions.explain: A single star is smallest; billions of stars form a galaxy (ours is the Milky Way); and all the galaxies together make up the Universe.

questions.lo: The Sun as a star, galaxies and the Universe
questions.q: Why can we see the planets in our solar system, such as Venus and Jupiter?
options: They make their own light like the Sun
They reflect light from the Sun
They are on fire
They give out light because they are so hot
questions.explain: Planets do not produce their own light. We see them because they reflect sunlight. Only stars, such as the Sun, make their own light.

questions.lo: Day and night from the Earth's rotation
questions.q: What causes day and night on Earth?
options: The Sun orbiting the Earth once a day
The Earth spinning on its axis once every 24 hours
The Moon covering the Sun
The Earth moving nearer to and further from the Sun
questions.explain: The Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the side facing away has night.

questions.lo: The seasons and the Earth's tilt
questions.q: What is the main cause of the seasons on Earth?
options: The Earth being closer to the Sun in summer
The tilt of the Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
The Sun giving out more heat in summer
The Earth spinning faster in summer
questions.explain: The seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis (about 23.5°). The tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere and how long the days are — not the distance from the Sun.

questions.lo: The seasons and the Earth's tilt
questions.q: When it is summer in the UK, it is winter in Australia at the same time. What does this prove?
options: The seasons are caused by distance from the Sun
The seasons are caused by the Earth's tilt, not distance
The Sun is hotter over the UK
Australia is further from the Sun all year
questions.explain: If distance caused the seasons, the whole Earth would be warm at once. Opposite seasons in the two hemispheres show the seasons come from the tilt, which makes one hemisphere lean towards the Sun while the other leans away.

questions.lo: The apparent daily and annual movement of the Sun and stars
questions.q: The Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west each day. What really causes this?
options: The Sun travelling across the sky
The Earth spinning on its axis
The Sun orbiting the Earth
Clouds moving across the sky
questions.explain: The Sun's daily path across the sky is an apparent motion. It is really the Earth's rotation that makes the Sun (and the stars at night) appear to move from east to west.

questions.lo: The light year as a unit of astronomical distance
questions.q: What does a light year measure?
options: The time it takes light to reach Earth
The distance light travels in one year
The age of a star
How long a planet takes to orbit the Sun
questions.explain: A light year is a unit of distance — the distance light travels in one year (about 9.5 million million km). Even though 'year' is in the name, it measures how far, not how long.

questions.lo: The light year as a unit of astronomical distance
questions.q: A star is said to be '30 light years away'. What is the best meaning of this?
options: The star is 30 years old
The star's distance from us is very large — the distance light covers in 30 years
The star will explode in 30 years
The star takes 30 years to spin once
questions.explain: Because a light year is a distance, '30 light years away' describes how far the star is. Light we see from it left the star 30 years ago, so we are seeing the past.

questions.lo: The difference between mass and weight
questions.q: A bag of shopping has a mass of 4 kg. Using g = 10 N/kg on Earth, which statement is correct?
options: Its weight is 4 N and its mass is 40 kg
Its weight is 40 N and its mass stays 4 kg anywhere
Its mass would become 40 kg on the Moon
Its weight is 0.4 N
questions.explain: W = m × g = 4 × 10 = 40 N. The mass stays 4 kg everywhere, but the weight would be smaller on the Moon because g is smaller there.
